replies.author: Tasty-Helicopter-411
replies.body:
layered responsibilities. I have my "chief of staff" who essentially is my AI director/plant manager/ big boss. his job is to make sure the work groups are doing what they are supposed to be doing. Are they doing their tasks, are they completing them, nothing gets dropped or forgotten or half-assed. Below him is the Team lead. He's built to be the subject matter expert in his field, but I don't want him bogged down doing everything himself, because that's how things get missed. Instead I tell him what his mission/purpose is. To become an expert in stock trading, then create a day trading team with a focus on taking profit. Instead of telling him who he needs to have on the team, I just tell him what I want them to accomplish and let him figure out who he will need instead. So he creates the team of bots under him. The technical analyst. The market trend analyst. The public perception analyst, two trading strategies researchers, etc. Then each is tasked to search the internet for examples of experts in their field and analyze what made these people great, them emulate them. These bots are all put into a Trading Team channel, which is effectively a group chat for bots. I connected the team lead to the TV MCP server, and all the analytical tools in it with the guidance that he is to distribute the information obtained to the appropriate expert of that topic. From that information, they can build a daily watchlist of stocks based upon upcoming earnings reports, news articles, negative events or publicity, world events that may impact operations or profits, etc. Waiting on my Trader Team lead to come back with the Pine Script and webhook to send alerts directly to the Team when they fire on TV. From there, if a stock is already on the watch list, and it fires an alert, the Team lead will have discretion to enter the trade given that the position is less than 50% of the account balance, preferably 20% - 30% per trade. A trade in excess of 50% but no more than 80% can only be executed if all team members agree that the trade is highly likely to be profitable, and my Chief of Staff approves the trade. Any/all trades that result in a loss of capital are a loss. All losses are logged until the end of the trading day, when the Team must review every loss and determine WHY it failed. What indicator was missed? what piece of information was overlooked? Was there a shift in the market or in the stock being traded that was overlooked? The team must determine the root cause for the failed trade and determine if a change needs to be made in how the responsible AI performs their job in order to prevent a similar failure. Live trading doesn't even begin until after the team has paper traded for at least 30 days profitably, learning and improving through these daily After Action Reviews. On day one of going live trading, CoS supervises trading. If the team loses over 30% of the account balance without taking any winning trades, CoS stops trading to conduct a strategy effectiveness analysis.  Essentially, did they just have really bad luck? Or is the trading strategy flawed? If it is flawed, the Team has to go basically restart and figure out what went wrong. If it was just really bad luck, the CoS can allow them to restart trading. Again, the emphasis is on scalping, volatility and trend trading, with rapid transitions in and out of trades. I'm not looking for them to hold the trades in order to maximize profits, I just want to see plus signs on the trades. If they catch a stock in an upswing near a low resistance band, buy in, and jump out after the stock moves up just a little bit, then that's acceptable. My brokerage doesn't charge commissions on common stock trades, so a small profit is still all profit. 

In summary, by making each bot focus on just one aspect of the trade, they can do that one aspect very well. By putting them all in a group chat, they can share their expert opinions on any potential trade. By making the Team lead the sole "trigger puller", the other bots can focus on being experts. By being outside of the entire process, my Chief of Staff can oversee the whole thing and make sure no steps get missed and everyone stays focused on the task at hand and abides by my stated guidance. If the Team starts to operate outside my guidance, he can stop the trading. 

All that being said, I still anticipate the first month of live trading being bloody as they go through trial by fire. So I plan on keeping the account balance to just a couple hundred bucks. It forces the Team lead to keep trades smaller, reducing overall potential losses. by the second month, they should have a decent feel for what they're doing. And if they do well, the growing account balance will reward them with more money to trade with.
